178.text:
Each GitHub release has prebuilt Linux binaries. To build one: cargo build --release
B=./target/release/roxy

$B check --config roxy.yaml      # validate; exits 1 with diagnostics
$B run   --config roxy.yaml      # start; edits to the file reload A minimal roxy.yaml, which allows GET and HEAD to example.com and
denies everything else: version: 1
listeners:
  - name: proxy
    bind: 127.0.0.1:3128
tls:
  ca_dir: ./ca                 # writable; the CA is generated here
rules:
  - id: example
    when: host == "example.com" and method in [GET, HEAD]
    then: allow run --state-dir DIR keeps state that must survive a restart. A config
that can quarantine roxy requires it.
178.title: Without the image

179.text:
roxy check validates a config. roxy rule test shows what the policy
does with a request you describe, without sending any traffic. roxy check --config roxy.yaml        # exits 1 with diagnostics
roxy rule test --config roxy.yaml GET https://api.github.com/repos/a/b
roxy rule test --config roxy.yaml --metric github_writes=30 POST https://api.github.com/repos/a/b/issues roxy rule test prints the matching rules, their effects and the
decision. When a respond rule answers, it also prints the answer's
status and headers. It exits 0 on allow or an answer, and 3 on deny. The request arrives on the
config's first listener. The rules see the request as roxy run would: the URL is normalised
(https://H.example./a/%2e/b/../c has host == "h.example" and
path == "/a/c"), and a request roxy would refuse as malformed exits 1
with the same reason.
179.title: Testing a policy

180.text: flag sets --client-ip, --header, --body the request --chunked a body of unknown length --metric id=value a metric's value; unset metrics are 0, and unavailable tests the fail-closed path --state key=value an entry in the state store --tag name a tag, set before the rules run --body-bytes, --response-body-bytes byte counts, for rules that read them --response-status, --response-header the response head, for rules that read it --ws-text, --ws-opcode, --ws-size, --ws-direction one WebSocket message roxy rule test --help lists every flag.
180.title: Describing the request

181.text:
To find out what a new deny rule would block before you turn it on, give
it the same when but only a tag:   - id: trial-no-gists
    when: host == "gist.github.com"
    then: { tag: trial-no-gists } A rule with no allow, deny, quarantine or respond does not change the
decision: other rules still decide the request. The tag is there so you
can find the requests it matched. Each one's request event in the
flow log carries it: {"event":"request","req":{"method":"GET","host":"gist.github.com","path":"/x"},
 "decision":"allow","rules":["github-reads","trial-no-gists"],
 "tags":["trial-no-gists"],"terminal_rule":"github-reads"} so grep '"trial-no-gists"' flow.jsonl lists them. Because a matching
deny always wins, each of these is a request the real rule would have
refused. When you are happy with what it catches, replace the tag with
deny.
181.title: Trialling a rule on live traffic

182.text:
An addon sees each request on its way to the rules and each response on
its way back to the client (addon model). The
simplest addon passes both through unchanged. This page shows that
addon in each kind, as a starting point to change.
182.title: Writing addons

183.text:
A WASM addon is a WebAssembly component. Write one in Rust with the
roxy-addon
SDK. The crate is not on crates.io, so depend on it from the repository: # Cargo.toml
[package]
name = "passthrough"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"

[lib]
crate-type = ["cdylib"]

[dependencies]
roxy-addon = { git = "https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy" } // src/lib.rs
use roxy_addon::prelude::*;

struct Passthrough;

impl Layer for Passthrough {
    fn init(_config: &str) -> Result<Self, String> {   // the addon's `config:`, as JSON
        Ok(Passthrough)
    }

    fn handle(&mut self, req: Request, next: Next) -> Response {
        next.run(req)
    }
}

roxy_addon::export!(Passthrough); Build it and point roxy at the component: rustup target add wasm32-wasip2
cargo build --release --target wasm32-wasip2 addons:
  - name: passthrough
    kind: wasm
    path: target/wasm32-wasip2/release/passthrough.wasm handle runs once per exchange. It gets the client's request and a
Next, and returns the response for the client: Request  { method, scheme, authority, path_with_query, headers, body }
Response { status, headers, body } next.run(req) passes the request on to the next addon or the rules, and
returns the response that comes back. Returning that response unchanged
passes everything through. A body passed on without being read never
enters the component, so this costs almost nothing. From there, a layer can change the request or the response, or answer
the client itself without calling next.run: fn handle(&mut self, req: Request, next: Next) -> Response {
    let req = req.map_body(|body| body.transform(redact_chunk));
    next.run(req)
} Body streams: read it as it arrives with transform (per chunk) or
pipe (with state, able to hold bytes back), or collect it with
read_to_end(cap). flow::* and call_endpoint reach roxy's
host services: tags, state, records, and
calls to configured endpoints. A panic fails the exchange closed. WebSockets need nothing extra: the request and response bodies carry
them. The test component
redact
is a complete streaming redactor.
183.title: A WASM layer

184.text:
A service layer is a WebSocket server that roxy connects to. It must
accept the subprotocol roxy.layer.v7. addons:
  - name: passthrough
    kind: service
    endpoint: layer
    endpoints:
      layer: { url: "http://127.0.0.1:9000", private_ok: true } Each exchange is a stream on the connection, and every message names its
stream. A GET arrives like this: {"stream":1,"type":"open","flow":"01M5…","layer":"passthrough","mode":"enforce", …}
{"stream":1,"type":"request","method":"GET","url":"http://example.com/","headers":[["accept","*/*"]]}
{"stream":1,"type":"request_end"} The service sends back the request to pass on, in the same shape. When
the response comes back from upstream, roxy sends it the same way, and
the service sends back the response for the client: {"stream":1,"type":"response","status":200,"headers":[["content-type","text/html"]]}
{"stream":1,"type":"credit","dir":"response","bytes":262144}
{"stream":1,"type":"response_end"} Body bytes come as binary frames between a head and its end: a 4-byte
stream id, a direction byte (0 request, 1 response), then the bytes.
credit tells the service how many more body bytes roxy will take from
it. To pass everything through unchanged, send every frame back exactly as it
arrived, except open and reset: import asyncio
import json

from websockets.asyncio.server import serve


async def layer(ws):
    async for frame in ws:
        if isinstance(frame, str) and json.loads(frame)["type"] in ("open", "reset"):
            continue
        await ws.send(frame)


async def main():
    async with serve(layer, "127.0.0.1", 9000, subprotocols=["roxy.layer.v7"]):
        await asyncio.Future()


asyncio.run(main()) This works because the service's replies have the same shape as what it
receives. Heads, body bytes, trailers and ends go back as the request and
response to pass on. Sending roxy's credit back gives roxy as much
credit as roxy gave the service, so roxy never sends more than the
service can pass on. open describes the exchange and needs no answer.
After a reset the stream is gone. This is for mode: enforce. An observer gets a copy of the exchange and
sends none of it back. The service layer protocol
covers both modes, flow control, errors and host-service calls. A real service usually wants each exchange as one task. The
quickstart's sidecar includes
roxy_layer.py,
a Python asyncio implementation of the protocol that handles the framing,
flow control and errors, and hands a handler one exchange at a time.
184.title: A service layer

185.text:
Any language that builds WebAssembly components can implement
wit/addon.wit,
the roxy:addon@0.3.0 package, whose comments document each call. Go and JavaScript produce larger, slower
components. Python in WASM bundles an interpreter and needs raised memory
limits. For Python with native dependencies, or anything that should run
in its own process, write a service layer instead. A component has no network, filesystem or environment access. Outbound
calls go through named endpoints, and output to stdout or stderr is
discarded: use flow.log. Build a component against the wit/ of the roxy version it runs on. A
component built against another version fails when the config loads,
naming the imports that do not match.
185.title: Other languages

186.text:
roxy understands HTTP, not any particular API. Logic that needs to
understand the traffic, such as checking a model's tool calls or counting
tokens, goes in an addon. Each addon is a step that the request passes
through on its way to the rules, and that the response passes back
through on its way to the client. An addon is either: a WASM layer (kind: wasm): a WebAssembly component that runs
inside roxy (writing addons); or a service layer (kind: service): an external service that each
exchange streams through over a WebSocket
(service layer protocol). Configuring addons is covered in
addon configuration.
186.title: Addon model

187.text:
Addons run in the order they are listed under addons:, between the
client and the rules. Nothing configurable runs between the rules and the
network, so whatever the rules approved is what leaves. All the steps run
at the same time on a stream, each working on the chunk the step before
it passed on.
187.title: The stack

188.text:
For each exchange, an addon gets the request as the step before it passed
it on. It can: pass the request on unchanged, or change it first; hold it, for example while a person approves it; answer the client itself, without passing the request on; do the same with the response on its way back. The request and response are handled separately, so an addon can start
answering before it has passed the request on, or while it still holds
it. An addon passes each request on at most once and answers exactly once.
To call anything else, such as a monitoring model, it uses a
named endpoint, which does
not go through the stack. An addon can ask for the head only, or the head and the body, in each
direction. A body it does not ask for goes past it untouched and costs
nothing (what a layer sees).
188.title: What an addon can do

189.text:
The rules judge every request that leaves. Whatever the last addon
passes on is checked as strictly as a client's request, and judged by
the rules as if the client had sent it. Addons are held to the client's limits. Header limits, body caps
and timeouts apply to what an addon passes on, as they do to a client. Failure is closed. An enforcing addon that fails makes the
exchange fail with 503. There is no "on error, pass"
(failure). An addon can replace any response on its way back, including a refusal
from the rules. Addons are trusted, the refused request never left, and
the flow log keeps the rules' decision.
189.title: Guarantees

190.text:
Traffic passes through the addons in order: the second addon sees what
the first passed on, in the order it passed it on. Calls to roxy's host services, such as
writing state or adding a tag, run alongside the traffic rather than in
it. If addon A writes state that addon B should read, A must wait for its
write to finish before passing on the bytes B will read them with. A WASM
addon's calls always finish before it carries on. A service layer waits
for the result itself. For the rules to see a tag or state write when they decide on the
request, it must land before the addon passes the request on. A later
write is seen by the next rule that reads it, but never changes a decision
already made.
190.title: Ordering across layers

191.text:
mode: enforce (the default): the addon is in the path, and what it
does takes effect. mode: observe: the addon gets a copy of the traffic and cannot change
or delay it. Its failures are logged, never fatal. This is the way to
try out a new monitor. An observer that falls too far behind loses its
copy, and the exchange carries on
(observers).
191.title: Modes

192.text:
An exchange is one request and its response. Every exchange takes the same
path, however roxy is deployed.
192.title: How roxy works

193.text:
On a proxy listener the client sends CONNECT, and roxy terminates the TLS
inside the tunnel with a certificate from its own CA. On a gateway
listener, a load balancer in front has already terminated TLS
(HTTP). roxy parses each request into one canonical form and sends that form
upstream. Ambiguous input is rejected rather than guessed at, so what the
addons and rules see is exactly what is forwarded. Bodies stay streams.
193.title: Decrypt and parse

194.text:
An addon is a WASM component that runs inside roxy or an external service
the traffic streams through. Addons run in the order they are configured
and can rewrite, hold, answer or block the exchange. Whatever an addon
passes on is checked again as strictly as a client request
(addon model).
194.title: Addons

195.text:
The rules are a list of allows, and denies that restrict them. A matching
deny always wins, and anything no rule allows is denied. The decision to
forward is made on the request head. Rules that read bodies or the
response are checked again as the bytes stream, and can still stop the
exchange (policy evaluation). secrets:
  openai: { env: OPENAI_API_KEY }

rules:
  - id: github-reads
    when: host under "github.com" and method in [GET, HEAD]
    then: allow

  - id: openai
    when: host == "api.openai.com" and path starts_with "/v1/" and method == POST
    then:
      - set_header: { authorization: "Bearer ${secret:openai}" }   # the client never sees the key
      - allow

  - id: upload-cap                         # checked as the body streams
    when: host == "api.openai.com" and body.bytes > 10mb
    then: { deny: { status: 413 } }
195.title: Rules

196.text:
roxy resolves the host itself and checks every address against the
address floor before it connects. A name that resolves to a private
address is refused unless a rule allows it
(upstream,
address floor).
196.title: Connect

197.text:
The response comes back the same way: rules that read it are checked, the
addons see it, and roxy re-frames it for the client.
197.title: Respond

198.text:
Every step writes to the flow log: one JSON line per exchange, naming the
rule that decided, the addons that ran and what changed. The log never
drops a record. When it falls behind, traffic waits
(flow log).
198.title: Log

199.text:
The compiled config is swapped in whole when it changes. An exchange
finishes under the config it started with
(reload). In node mode
the config comes from a control plane instead of a file.
199.title: Reloads

200.text:
On ordinary HTTP traffic roxy is on a par with Envoy. Doing TLS
interception it handles 3 to 20 times the requests per core of mitmproxy,
with a median latency in milliseconds rather than hundreds of
milliseconds. requests per core, roxy relative to 1 KiB 64 KiB 1 MiB Envoy, as a gateway 1.3x 1.0x 0.8x Envoy, as an egress proxy 1.5x 1.3x 1.3x mitmproxy, doing TLS interception 19x 8x 2.7x
200.title: Performance

201.text:
roxy spends about 100 µs of CPU on a small exchange with no addons. An
addon that does nothing adds roughly another 100 µs, whether it is a WASM
component or a service. So an addon that does T µs of work makes an
exchange cost about 200 + T µs: four cores give roughly 20,000 requests a
second with no work, 13,000 at 100 µs and 4,000 at 800 µs. A service
layer's own CPU comes on top. Bodies cost about 3 µs per KiB through a WASM layer and 4.5 µs per KiB
through a service layer, even when the layer leaves them untouched. A
1 MiB response through a do-nothing layer costs 4 to 5 ms, against about
0.6 ms with no addons. throughput lost to a do-nothing layer, as an egress proxy 1 KiB 64 KiB 1 MiB WASM layer about 50% about 70% about 85% service layer (sidecar on localhost) about 60% about 75% about 90%
201.title: What an addon costs

202.text:
These figures come from one machine. No run uses body rules, capture,
body digests or a real addon. A body digest costs about one core per
400 MB/s on a CPU without SHA extensions, which is why it is opt-in.
202.title: What is not measured

203.text:
The policy is a list of rules. Each rule has an id, a when condition
written in the rule language, and a then
saying what to do (actions): rules:
  - id: github-reads
    when: host under "github.com" and method in [GET, HEAD]
    then: allow

  - id: no-admin-paths
    when: path starts_with "/admin"
    then: deny

  - id: upload-cap
    when: body.bytes > 10mb
    then: deny
203.title: Policy evaluation

204.text:
roxy checks every rule against the request. If any matching rule denies,
the request is denied. If none denies and at least one allows, it is
allowed. If no rule matches, it is denied. The order of the rules makes
no difference to the decision. With the rules above, GET https://github.com/admin matches both
github-reads and no-admin-paths, and is denied. A rule can also answer the request itself with respond, and roxy then
dials nothing (actions). A matching
deny or quarantine still wins over it. A respond decides the request alone, so it cannot share it. A matching
respond beside a matching allow, or two matching respond rules, are
a conflict: the request is refused with 503, terminal_rule is
_fail_closed and the flow log reason is terminal_conflict. No order
of the two rules makes both right, and picking one would make the
decision depend on where the rules sit. Write the rules so they do not
match the same request, for example with not (path == "/oauth/token")
in the allow.
204.title: Deny wins

205.text:
roxy decides whether to forward a request as soon as it has the request
head, before any of the body has been sent on. Most rules are decided
then. Some rules read things that are only known later, such as how many body
bytes have been sent (body.bytes) or the response status. roxy checks
these rules again each time the value changes. In the example,
upload-cap is checked as the body streams, and stops the upload once it
passes 10 MiB. The reference calls the first kind admission rules and the second
in-flight rules. roxy check and roxy rule test say which each rule
is. A rule checked later can only deny, because by then the request has
already gone. It cannot allow or respond. It can also log, tag, write state, or change response
headers that have not been sent yet. When it denies, roxy stops the
exchange: the client gets an error if its response has not started, and
otherwise the connection is closed. A rule that reads the whole body (body.text) is different: roxy holds
the body back until it has read it, and then decides
(body rules).
205.title: When rules run

206.text:
Order matters for what rules change, not for the decision. When a
request is allowed, every matching rule's changes apply from top to
bottom, so if two rules set the same header, the lower one wins. When a
respond rule answers, nothing is forwarded, so changes to the request do
nothing; log, set_state, tag, and capture or digest of the
response still apply. The flow log names the rule that decided as
terminal_rule. A tag set by a rule can only be read by rules below it. roxy rejects a
config where a rule reads a tag that a rule further down sets.
206.title: Effects

207.text:
If a rule needs a value roxy cannot get, such as a metric when its table
is full or an address list that failed to load, the request is denied
with 503. roxy never guesses that the condition was false. A value that
is just absent, like a header the client did not send, is null and
compares normally
(missing values).
207.title: When an input is missing

208.text:
roxy is a security boundary for the HTTP traffic that reaches it. The
guarantees on this page decide the behaviour described everywhere else.
208.title: Threat model and guarantees

209.text:
The attacker is the client. It controls every byte it sends to roxy,
may run arbitrary code, and may have root inside its own container or VM. Trusted: the host, roxy's binary and config (addons included), the
secrets roxy holds, the public CA roots used to verify upstreams, the
upstreams the rules allow, and the load balancers a listener's
forwarded_for counts. Upstream responses are not treated as hostile,
but roxy still bounds their size and time and re-frames them. For traffic that reaches it, roxy prevents: reaching any destination the rules do not allow, including through
Host or SNI spoofing, DNS rebinding, redirects to private addresses,
CONNECT to arbitrary ports, or non-HTTP protocols inside CONNECT; request smuggling and desync through ambiguous framing, on either side
of roxy; exfiltrating real credentials: with secret injection the client only
holds placeholders; unbounded memory or connection use from slow clients, huge headers,
huge bodies and key churn, within the configured limits; learning anything from a deny beyond the rule id. roxy does not prevent traffic that never reaches it, timing or DNS
side channels from the workload, compromise of an upstream the rules
allow, or compromise of the host. WASM addons have memory and time limits
but no total CPU budget, so addon configuration must be trusted.
209.title: Threat model

210.text:
roxy decides what passes through it. It cannot stop traffic that goes
around it. Sandbox containment claims that all of the workload's traffic goes
through roxy. The network makes that true: the workload must have no
route out except roxy's proxy port
(sandbox containment). An HTTP gateway makes no such claim. It governs the requests sent to
it, and clients keep any other routes they have
(HTTP gateway).
210.title: Which use case claims what

211.text:
In node mode a node proves who it is with a bearer
token that the control plane issued at enrolment. The token stops a host
that was never enrolled, or one that has been revoked, from getting a
policy or secrets. It does not protect against the host roxy runs on:
whatever can read the state dir can use the token until it expires or the
node is revoked.
211.title: Node identity

212.text:
Anything roxy cannot parse, verify or classify is refused. An empty rule
set denies everything, and so does an expired policy. A config that fails
to load is not applied, and a failed reload keeps the running policy. A
policy input that is unavailable, such as a full metric table, denies the
exchange rather than making a condition false. An enforcing addon that
fails denies the exchange. Resource limits
lists every case.
212.title: Fail closed

213.text:
roxy parses each request into a strict model and writes it out again in
one unambiguous form. Nothing the client sends reaches the upstream
byte for byte, and what the rules match is exactly what is forwarded
(HTTP).
213.title: Canonical re-serialisation

214.text:
A matching deny wins over any matching allow, wherever it sits in the
list. Rule order affects effects, never decisions, so adding a deny can
only narrow what passes (policy evaluation).
214.title: Deny always wins

215.text:
Bounded tables, such as metric series and the state store, never evict
entries to make room. A request that needs a new entry in a full table is
denied, so a client cannot reset its own rate limit by churning keys.
215.title: Never evict

216.text:
The flow log and capture never drop a record. When a log falls behind or
its disk fails, roxy holds traffic until it catches up
(flow log).
216.title: Audit backpressure

217.text:
Addons run before the rules and can reshape traffic freely. Whatever they
pass on is validated like a client request and judged by the rules as if
the client had sent it. Nothing configurable runs between the rules and
the network, and the address floor checks the address actually dialled. An addon can still change the response the client gets, including a
refusal from the rules: addons are trusted, the request did not leave,
and the flow log records the rules' decision.
217.title: The rules judge everything that leaves

218.text:
A body is buffered only when a rule or addon needs to read it, up to a
cap, and all buffers together stay within one process-wide budget
(limits). Memory use does not grow with
body size.
218.title: Streams, not messages

219.text:
Strictness is aimed at malformed or ambiguous traffic. A conforming client
doing ordinary things (large uploads, keep-alive, 100-continue,
WebSockets, compression) through an allowed rule should notice nothing
except the CA. A default that breaks a conforming client is a bug.
219.title: Well-behaved clients work
